{"id": "i7", "chunks": [{"file": "/home/arnold/arnold/github/notes-helper/backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/refs/textbook.md", "start": 132, "end": 175, "text": "For example, a spanning set for the vector space $\\mathbf{C}^{2}$ is the set\n\n$$\n\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle \\equiv\\left[\\begin{array}{l}\n1  \\tag{2.5}\\\\\n0\n\\end{array}\\right] ; \\quad\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle \\equiv\\left[\\begin{array}{l}\n0 \\\\\n1\n\\end{array}\\right]\n$$\n\nsince any vector\n\n$$\n|v\\rangle=\\left[\\begin{array}{l}\na_{1}  \\tag{2.6}\\\\\na_{2}\n\\end{array}\\right]\n$$\n\nin $\\mathbf{C}^{2}$ can be written as a linear combination $|v\\rangle=a_{1}\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle+a_{2}\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle$ of the vectors $\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle$ and $\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle$.\nWe say that the vectors $\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle$ and $\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle$ span the vector space $\\mathbf{C}^{2}$.\n\nGenerally, a vector space may have many different spanning sets.\nA second spanning set for the vector space $\\mathbf{C}^{2}$ is the set\n\n$$\n\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle \\equiv \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\left[\\begin{array}{l}\n1  \\tag{2.7}\\\\\n1\n\\end{array}\\right] ; \\quad\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle \\equiv \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{2}}\\left[\\begin{array}{r}\n1 \\\\\n-1\n\\end{array}\\right]\n$$\n\nsince an arbitrary vector $|v\\rangle=\\left(a_{1}, a_{2}\\right)$ can be written as a linear combination of $\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle$ and $\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle$,\n\n$$\n\\begin{equation*}\n|v\\rangle=\\frac{a_{1}+a_{2}}{\\sqrt{2}}\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle+\\frac{a_{1}-a_{2}}{\\sqrt{2}}\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle .\n\\tag{2.8}\n\\end{equation*}"}]}
{"id": "i8", "chunks": [{"file": "/home/arnold/arnold/github/notes-helper/backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/refs/textbook.md", "start": 178, "end": 191, "text": "A set of non-zero vectors $\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle, \\ldots,\\left|v_{n}\\right\\rangle$ are linearly dependent if there exists a set of complex numbers $a_{1}, \\ldots, a_{n}$ with $a_{i} \\neq 0$ for at least one value of $i$, such that\n\n$$\n\\begin{equation*}\na_{1}\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle+a_{2}\\left|v_{2}\\right\\rangle+\\cdots+a_{n}\\left|v_{n}\\right\\rangle=0 \\tag{2.9}\n\\end{equation*}\n$$\n\nA set of vectors is linearly independent if it is not linearly dependent.\nIt can be shown that any two sets of linearly independent vectors which span a vector space $V$ contain the same number of elements.\nWe call such a set a basis for $V$.\nFurthermore, such a basis set always exists.\nThe number of elements in the basis is defined to be the dimension of $V$.\nIn this book we will only be interested in finite dimensional vector spaces."}]}
{"id": "i10", "chunks": [{"file": "/home/arnold/arnold/github/notes-helper/backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/refs/textbook.md", "start": 199, "end": 214, "text": "A linear operator between vector spaces $V$ and $W$ is defined to be any function $A$ : $V \\rightarrow W$ which is linear in its inputs,\n\n$$\n\\begin{equation*}\nA\\left(\\sum_{i} a_{i}\\left|v_{i}\\right\\rangle\\right)=\\sum_{i} a_{i} A\\left(\\left|v_{i}\\right\\rangle\\right) .\n\\tag{2.10}\n\\end{equation*}\n$$\n\nUsually we just write $A|v\\rangle$ to denote $A(|v\\rangle)$.\nWhen we say that a linear operator $A$ is defined on a vector space, $V$, we mean that $A$ is a linear operator from $V$ to $V$.\nAn important linear operator on any vector space $V$ is the identity operator, $I_{V}$, defined by the equation $I_{V}|v\\rangle \\equiv|v\\rangle$ for all vectors $|v\\rangle$.\nWhere no chance of confusion arises we drop the subscript $V$ and just write $I$ to denote the identity operator.\nAnother important linear operator is the zero operator, which we denote 0 .\nThe zero operator maps all vectors to\nthe zero vector, $0|v\\rangle \\equiv 0$."}]}

{"id": "i14", "chunks": [{"file": "/home/arnold/arnold/github/notes-helper/backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/refs/textbook.md", "start": 267, "end": 293, "text": "Four extremely useful matrices which we shall often have occasion to use are the Pauli matrices.\nThese are 2 by 2 matrices, which go by a variety of notations.\nThe matrices, and their corresponding notations, are depicted in Figure 2.2.\nThe Pauli matrices are so useful in the study of quantum computation and quantum information that we encourage you to memorize them by working through in detail the many examples and exercises based upon them in subsequent sections.\n\n$$\n\\begin{aligned}\n\\sigma_{0} \\equiv I \\equiv\\left[\\begin{array}{ll}\n1 & 0 \\\\\n0 & 1\n\\end{array}\\right] & \\sigma_{1} \\equiv \\sigma_{x} \\equiv X \\equiv\\left[\\begin{array}{ll}\n0 & 1 \\\\\n1 & 0\n\\end{array}\\right] \\\\\n\\sigma_{2} \\equiv \\sigma_{y} \\equiv Y \\equiv\\left[\\begin{array}{rr}\n0 & -i \\\\\ni & 0\n\\end{array}\\right] & \\sigma_{3} \\equiv \\sigma_{z} \\equiv Z \\equiv\\left[\\begin{array}{rr}\n1 & 0 \\\\\n0 & -1\n\\end{array}\\right]\n\\end{aligned}\n$$\n\nFigure 2.2.\nThe Pauli matrices.\nSometimes $I$ is omitted from the list with just $X, Y$ and $Z$ known as the Pauli matrices."}]}
{"id": "i16", "chunks": [{"file": "/home/arnold/arnold/github/notes-helper/backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/refs/textbook.md", "start": 297, "end": 300, "text": "An inner product is a function which takes as input two vectors $|v\\rangle$ and $|w\\rangle$ from a vector space and produces a complex number as output.\nFor the time being, it will be convenient to write the inner product of $|v\\rangle$ and $|w\\rangle$ as $(|v\\rangle,|w\\rangle)$.\nThis is not the standard quantum mechanical notation; for pedagogical clarity the ( $\\cdot, \\cdot$ ) notation will be useful occasionally in this chapter.\nThe standard quantum mechanical notation for the inner product $(|v\\rangle,|w\\rangle)$ is $\\langle v \\mid w\\rangle$, where $|v\\rangle$ and $|w\\rangle$ are vectors in the inner product space, and the notation $\\langle v|$ is used for the dual vector to the vector $|v\\rangle$; the dual is a linear operator from the inner product space $V$ to the complex numbers $\\mathbf{C}$, defined by $\\langle v|(|w\\rangle) \\equiv\\langle v \\mid w\\rangle \\equiv(|v\\rangle,|w\\rangle)$."}, {"file": "/home/arnold/arnold/github/notes-helper/backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/refs/textbook.md", "start": 326, "end": 326, "text": "We call a vector space equipped with an inner product an inner product space."}]}

{"id": "i21", "chunks": [{"file": "/home/arnold/arnold/github/notes-helper/backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/refs/textbook.md", "start": 343, "end": 357, "text": "Vectors $|w\\rangle$ and $|v\\rangle$ are orthogonal if their inner product is zero.\nFor example, $|w\\rangle \\equiv (1,0)$ and $|v\\rangle \\equiv(0,1)$ are orthogonal with respect to the inner product defined by (2.14).\nWe define the norm of a vector $|v\\rangle$ by\n\n$$\n\\begin{equation*}\n\\||v\\rangle \\| \\equiv \\sqrt{\\langle v \\mid v\\rangle} .\n\\tag{2.16}\n\\end{equation*}\n$$\n\nA unit vector is a vector $|v\\rangle$ such that $\\||v\\rangle \\|=1$.\nWe also say that $|v\\rangle$ is normalized if $\\||v\\rangle \\|=1$.\nIt is convenient to talk of normalizing a vector by dividing by its norm; thus $|v\\rangle / \\||v\\rangle \\|$ is the normalized form of $|v\\rangle$, for any non-zero vector $|v\\rangle$.\nA set $|i\\rangle$ of vectors with index $i$ is orthonormal if each vector is a unit vector, and distinct vectors in the set are orthogonal, that is, $\\langle i \\mid j\\rangle=\\delta_{i j}$, where $i$ and $j$ are both chosen from the index set."}]}
{"id": "i22", "chunks": [{"file": "/home/arnold/arnold/github/notes-helper/backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/refs/textbook.md", "start": 362, "end": 373, "text": "Suppose $\\left|w_{1}\\right\\rangle, \\ldots,\\left|w_{d}\\right\\rangle$ is a basis set for some vector space $V$ with an inner product.\nThere is a useful method, the Gram-Schmidt procedure, which can be used to produce an orthonormal basis set $\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle, \\ldots,\\left|v_{d}\\right\\rangle$ for the vector space $V$.\nDefine $\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle \\equiv\\left|w_{1}\\right\\rangle / \\|\\left|w_{1}\\right\\rangle \\|$, and for $1 \\leq k \\leq d-1$ define $\\left|v_{k+1}\\right\\rangle$ inductively by\n\n$$\n\\begin{equation*}\n\\left|v_{k+1}\\right\\rangle \\equiv \\frac{\\left|w_{k+1}\\right\\rangle-\\sum_{i=1}^{k}\\left\\langle v_{i} \\mid w_{k+1}\\right\\rangle\\left|v_{i}\\right\\rangle}{\\|\\left|w_{k+1}\\right\\rangle-\\sum_{i=1}^{k}\\left\\langle v_{i} \\mid w_{k+1}\\right\\rangle\\left|v_{i}\\right\\rangle \\|} \\tag{2.17}\n\\end{equation*}\n$$\n\nIt is not difficult to verify that the vectors $\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle, \\ldots,\\left|v_{d}\\right\\rangle$ form an orthonormal set which is also a basis for $V$.\nThus, any finite dimensional vector space of dimension $d$ has an orthonormal basis, $\\left|v_{1}\\right\\rangle, \\ldots,\\left|v_{d}\\right\\rangle$."}]}
{"id": "i24", "chunks": [{"file": "/home/arnold/arnold/github/notes-helper/backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/refs/textbook.md", "start": 380, "end": 396, "text": "With these conventions, the inner product on a Hilbert space can be given a convenient matrix representation.\nLet $|w\\rangle=\\sum_{i} w_{i}|i\\rangle$ and $|v\\rangle=\\sum_{j} v_{j}|j\\rangle$ be representations of vectors $|w\\rangle$ and $|v\\rangle$ with respect to some orthonormal basis $|i\\rangle$.\nThen, since $\\langle i \\mid j\\rangle=\\delta_{i j}$,\n\n$$\n\\begin{align*}\n\\langle v \\mid w\\rangle & =\\left(\\sum_{i} v_{i}|i\\rangle, \\sum_{j} w_{j}|j\\rangle\\right)=\\sum_{i j} v_{i}^{*} w_{j} \\delta_{i j}=\\sum_{i} v_{i}^{*} w_{i}  \\tag{2.18}\\\\\n& =\\left[v_{1}^{*} \\ldots v_{n}^{*}\\right]\\left[\\begin{array}{c}\nw_{1} \\\\\n\\vdots \\\\\nw_{n}\n\\end{array}\\right] \\tag{2.19}\n\\end{align*}\n$$\n\nThat is, the inner product of two vectors is equal to the vector inner product between two matrix representations of those vectors, provided the representations are written with respect to the same orthonormal basis.\nWe also see that the dual vector $\\langle v|$ has a nice interpretation as the row vector whose components are complex conjugates of the corresponding components of the column vector representation of $|v\\rangle$."}]}

{"id": "i30", "chunks": [{"file": "/home/arnold/arnold/github/notes-helper/backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/refs/textbook.md", "start": 485, "end": 493, "text": "An eigenvector of a linear operator $A$ on a vector space is a non-zero vector $|v\\rangle$ such that $A|v\\rangle=v|v\\rangle$, where $v$ is a complex number known as the eigenvalue of $A$ corresponding to $|v\\rangle$.\nIt will often be convenient to use the notation $v$ both as a label for the eigenvector, and to represent the eigenvalue.\nWe assume that you are familiar with the elementary properties of eigenvalues and eigenvectors - in particular, how to find them, via the characteristic equation.\nThe characteristic function is defined to be $c(\\lambda) \\equiv \\operatorname{det}|A-\\lambda I|$,\nwhere det is the determinant function for matrices; it can be shown that the characteristic function depends only upon the operator $A$, and not on the specific matrix representation used for $A$.\nThe solutions of the characteristic equation $c(\\lambda)=0$ are the eigenvalues of the operator $A$.\nBy the fundamental theorem of algebra, every polynomial has at least one complex root, so every operator $A$ has at least one eigenvalue, and a corresponding eigenvector.\nThe eigenspace corresponding to an eigenvalue $v$ is the set of vectors which have eigenvalue $v$.\nIt is a vector subspace of the vector space on which $A$ acts."}]}
{"id": "i31", "chunks": [{"file": "/home/arnold/arnold/github/notes-helper/backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/refs/textbook.md", "start": 495, "end": 508, "text": "A diagonal representation for an operator $A$ on a vector space $V$ is a representation $A=\\sum_{i} \\lambda_{i}|i\\rangle\\langle i|$, where the vectors $|i\\rangle$ form an orthonormal set of eigenvectors for $A$, with corresponding eigenvalues $\\lambda_{i}$.\nAn operator is said to be diagonalizable if it has a diagonal representation.\nIn the next section we will find a simple set of necessary and sufficient conditions for an operator on a Hilbert space to be diagonalizable.\nAs an example of a diagonal representation, note that the Pauli $Z$ matrix may be written\n\n$$\nZ=\\left[\\begin{array}{rr}\n1 & 0  \\tag{2.29}\\\\\n0 & -1\n\\end{array}\\right]=|0\\rangle\\langle 0|-|1\\rangle\\langle 1|\n$$\n\nwhere the matrix representation is with respect to orthonormal vectors $|0\\rangle$ and $|1\\rangle$, respectively.\nDiagonal representations are sometimes also known as orthonormal decompositions."}]}
{"id": "i32", "chunks": [{"file": "/home/arnold/arnold/github/notes-helper/backend/projects/0728ff4c758a/refs/textbook.md", "start": 510, "end": 522, "text": "When an eigenspace is more than one dimensional we say that it is degenerate.\nFor example, the matrix $A$ defined by\n\n$$\nA \\equiv\\left[\\begin{array}{lll}\n2 & 0 & 0  \\tag{2.30}\\\\\n0 & 2 & 0 \\\\\n0 & 0 & 0\n\\end{array}\\right]\n$$\n\nhas a two-dimensional eigenspace corresponding to the eigenvalue 2 .\nThe eigenvectors $(1,0,0)$ and $(0,1,0)$ are said to be degenerate because they are linearly independent eigenvectors of $A$ with the same eigenvalue."}]}
